newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: BIS cites concern on asset price gains.
newsitem.headline: BIS cites concern on asset price gains.

text.p: Strong gains in financial markets in the past year have raised some concern about whether price increases can be sustained, the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) said in its annual report.
In its 67th annual report, it said that the price increases in bonds, as well as stocks, deserved attention.

"Against a backdrop of generally subdued economic growth and low inflation, bond and equity markets recorded large gains last year. Yet even though fundamentals currently seem favourable, there is concern that price advances in some markets could contain an unstable element," BIS said.

Recent gains in the bond markets whose countries are seeking membership to the single European currency, foreseen as the third stage of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), may also reflect some unstable elements, it said.
Potential members of the currency must meet standards laid under the Treaty of Maastricht signed February 1992 by European Union finance and foreign ministers.

"The strong convergence of bond yields in Europe, and the sharp declines in rates in the historically high-yielding markets, suggest that part of the explanation for the recent gains in asset values may be an increased appetite for risk which might easily be reversed," BIS said.

The convergence of long-term interest rates among European bonds has led to lower yields which help countries to fulfil Maastricht fiscal criteria by reducing their debt burden and offsetting some of the negative impact of necessary fiscal consolidation.

"However, by the same token this conditionality also increases the vulnerability to adversely shifting market expectations if uncertainty remains regarding the fulfilment of the inflation and fiscal conditions," BIS said.
It added that "the possibility remains that in the current environment of low interest rates a search for high yields has led to an excessive convergence of bond yields."
That is, countries which might otherwise have had higher bond yields have drawn investors seeking higher returns. This has pulled down yields on those countries.
With respect to equity prices, BIS said that some of the price advances reflected strong growth in corporate earnings.
"However, there is more to the generalised run-up in share prices than strong corporate profits," BIS said.
It noted that price/earnings ratios for most markets, including the U.S., were above their 1986/1995 averages, and were at record levels in the Netherlands and Switzerland.

Some of this may reflect lower inflation rates, which has reduced equity risk premiums. It may also be linked to lower real interest rates, as well as increased numbers of share buybacks. But BIS also said price/earnings ratios seem more pronounced if respective business cycles are taken into account.

"Multiples typically peak during the early stages of a cyclical recovery, when there is the potential for above-average profit growth over the medium-term. By this standard, the price/earnings multiples for the Dutch and U.S. markets during March 1997 seem relatively high by historical standards, given that both economies were operating approximately at potential," BIS said.
